helping-someone.title: Helping someone else
helping-someone.intro: You do not need to be an expert. A calm conversation, listening carefully and helping someone reach the right support can make a real difference.

blocks.heading: Signs somebody may be struggling
items: Changes in mood, behaviour, attendance or appearance
Withdrawal from teammates, colleagues, friends or family
Loss of confidence, motivation or enjoyment
Increased alcohol, drug or gambling behaviour
Comments about hopelessness, self-harm or suicide

blocks.heading: How to start the conversation
items: Choose a private and suitable time
Say what you have noticed without judging them
Ask: “How are you really doing?”
Listen more than you speak
Ask what support would feel helpful
Check in again afterwards

blocks.heading: What not to do
items: Do not dismiss their feelings or tell them simply to be stronger
Do not promise secrecy where somebody may be at risk
Do not try to diagnose them
Do not leave somebody alone when there is immediate danger

blocks.heading: Where to get help
items: Club Welfare Officer
Trusted manager, coach or senior club contact
Club medical or player-care staff
GP, NHS 111 or a specialist support service
999 or A&E in an emergency

remember.title: Remember
remember.body: Asking directly about suicide does not put the idea into somebody's head. If you are concerned, ask clearly, listen calmly and seek urgent help when needed.

mental-health.title: Looking after your mental health
mental-health.intro: Everyone has mental health. It can change over time and may be affected by pressure, injury, relationships, work, education and events away from football.

headings: You may find this page helpful if…

blocks.heading: You may find this page helpful if…
items: You feel different from your usual self
You are finding it harder to enjoy football or daily life
Your sleep, appetite, energy or concentration have changed
You want practical ways to protect your wellbeing

blocks.heading: Why this matters
paras: Good mental health supports concentration, confidence, decision-making, relationships, recovery and enjoyment of football. Difficulties can affect anyone, regardless of their role or level in the game.

blocks.heading: Signs to look out for
items: Persistent worry, sadness or irritability
Changes in sleep, appetite or energy
Withdrawing from teammates, colleagues, friends or family
Loss of motivation or enjoyment
Using alcohol, drugs, gambling or other behaviours to cope

blocks.heading: Things you can do today
items: Talk to someone you trust
Keep regular routines for sleep, food, hydration and movement
Break problems into smaller, manageable steps
Stay connected with people outside football
Seek professional help if difficulties persist or affect everyday life

blocks.heading: When should I seek help?
items: Symptoms have lasted for around two weeks or more
They are affecting football, work, education, relationships or daily life
They are getting worse or your usual coping strategies are not helping
You are worried about yourself or somebody else

stress-anxiety.title: Stress and anxiety
stress-anxiety.intro: Stress is the body's response to pressure. Anxiety can involve continuing worry, fear or physical symptoms even after the immediate pressure has passed.

headings: You may find this page helpful if…

blocks.heading: You may find this page helpful if…
items: You are struggling to switch off
Football or life feels overwhelming
You are constantly worrying
You have physical symptoms such as tension or a racing heart

blocks.heading: Why this matters
paras: Selection, contracts, performance, injury, travel, social media and balancing football with work, education or family life can all create pressure.

blocks.heading: Signs to look out for
items: Racing thoughts or constant worry
Tension, headaches, nausea or a racing heart
Poor sleep
Irritability or avoiding situations
Difficulty concentrating or making decisions

blocks.heading: Things you can do today
items: Slow your breathing and focus on the present
Write down what is within your control
Plan recovery time after matches and travel
Reduce caffeine and avoid using alcohol to cope
Speak to someone early rather than waiting for a crisis

depression.title: Depression and low mood
depression.intro: Low mood is common after disappointment or stress. Depression is more persistent and can affect thoughts, sleep, appetite, confidence, relationships and everyday functioning.

headings: You may find this page helpful if…

blocks.heading: You may find this page helpful if…
items: You have felt low for a while
You have lost interest in things you normally enjoy
You feel hopeless, guilty or worthless
Your mood is affecting football, work or relationships

blocks.heading: Why this matters
paras: Release, injury, non-selection, criticism and uncertainty can affect identity and confidence. Depression is an illness, not a lack of toughness or commitment.

blocks.heading: Signs to look out for
items: Low mood most days
Loss of interest or enjoyment
Hopelessness, guilt or feeling worthless
Low energy and poor concentration
Thoughts of death, suicide or self-harm

blocks.heading: Things you can do today
items: Tell someone what is happening
Maintain basic routines even when motivation is low
Avoid isolating yourself
Book an appointment with your GP
Use urgent help immediately if you may harm yourself

crisis.title: Suicidal thoughts and crisis support
crisis.intro: Suicidal thoughts can affect anyone and should always be taken seriously. Help is available and nobody should manage this alone.

headings: You may find this page helpful if…

blocks.heading: You may find this page helpful if…
items: You are thinking about suicide or self-harm
You feel trapped, hopeless or unable to cope
You are worried that someone else may be unsafe
You need urgent support now

blocks.heading: Why this matters
paras: Football pressures may add to personal difficulties, but suicide is rarely caused by one issue. A caring and direct conversation can help someone access support.

blocks.heading: Signs to look out for
items: Talking about wanting to die or being a burden
Feeling trapped, hopeless or unable to cope
Giving away possessions or saying goodbye
Sudden withdrawal or a major change in behaviour
Making plans or searching for methods

blocks.heading: Things you can do today
items: Call 999 if there is immediate danger
Go to A&E or contact NHS 111 for urgent help
Stay with the person where it is safe to do so
Listen calmly and take them seriously
Do not promise secrecy when somebody may be at risk

sleep.title: Sleep and recovery
sleep.intro: Sleep supports physical recovery, concentration, mood, immunity and decision-making.

headings: You may find this page helpful if…

blocks.heading: You may find this page helpful if…
items: You are struggling to fall asleep or stay asleep
You feel exhausted during the day
Your mood or concentration is affected
Travel, evening fixtures or worry are disrupting recovery

blocks.heading: Why this matters
paras: Evening fixtures, travel, adrenaline, pain and irregular routines can disrupt sleep. Poor sleep can affect reaction time, mood, recovery and performance.

blocks.heading: Signs to look out for
items: Difficulty falling or staying asleep
Daytime fatigue
Poor concentration or slower reactions
Irritability or low mood
Increasing reliance on caffeine, alcohol or medication

blocks.heading: Things you can do today
items: Keep regular sleep and wake times where possible
Create a wind-down routine after evening fixtures
Reduce caffeine later in the day
Avoid alcohol as a sleep aid
Seek medical advice for persistent insomnia or heavy snoring

gambling.title: Gambling and betting harms
gambling.intro: Football's connection with betting can make gambling feel normal. Harm can affect finances, relationships, mental health, employment and integrity responsibilities.

headings: You may find this page helpful if…

blocks.heading: You may find this page helpful if…
items: You are gambling more than you planned
You are chasing losses or hiding gambling
Money worries are increasing
Gambling is affecting football, work or relationships

blocks.heading: Why this matters
paras: People working in football may be subject to strict betting rules. Gambling can also create disciplinary, safeguarding and financial concerns.

blocks.heading: Signs to look out for
items: Chasing losses
Hiding gambling
Borrowing money to bet
Betting to escape stress or low mood
Missing training, work or family commitments

blocks.heading: Things you can do today
items: Stop and put practical blocks in place
Tell someone you trust
Do not borrow money to recover losses
Use bank, device and self-exclusion controls
Seek specialist help early

blocks.heading: When should I seek help?

alcohol-drugs.title: Alcohol and drugs
alcohol-drugs.intro: Alcohol and drug misuse can affect sleep, mood, judgement, relationships, fitness, conduct and injury recovery.

headings: You may find this page helpful if…

blocks.heading: You may find this page helpful if…
items: You are drinking or using drugs more often
You use alcohol or drugs to cope, relax or sleep
Your mood, relationships or performance are affected
You are worried about medication or supplement use

blocks.heading: Why this matters
paras: Substance use may affect attendance, performance, safety and anti-doping responsibilities. It can also become a way of coping with stress, injury or low mood.

blocks.heading: Signs to look out for
items: Using more often or in larger amounts
Needing alcohol or drugs to relax, cope or sleep
Mood changes, irritability or aggression
Declining attendance, motivation or performance
Hiding use or experiencing financial, legal or relationship problems

blocks.heading: Things you can do today
items: Avoid recreational drugs
Stay within UK low-risk alcohol guidance
Do not mix alcohol with medication without professional advice
Seek medical advice before suddenly stopping if dependent
Check medication and supplements against anti-doping requirements

welcome.h1: Whatever you’re facing today, you don’t have to face it alone.
welcome.body: The National League Wellbeing Hub provides trusted information, practical self-help and clear routes to support for players, staff and volunteers across National League football. It may also help families, friends and colleagues who are worried about someone.

urgent: If you are in crisis or worried about someone's safety, get help now.
